title: Leveling Expectations
summary: What separates a mid-level answer from a senior or staff+ answer to the same system design question, and how to calibrate your depth to the role.

slides.markdown:
The exact same question — "design a rate limiter," say — is scored against a different bar depending on the level you're interviewing for. A mid-level candidate and a staff candidate can both give a "correct" answer and still be scored very differently, because correctness is the floor at every level, not the ceiling.

This topic breaks down what each level actually adds on top of correctness, and how to calibrate your own answer's depth to the role you're in the room for.

slides.sectionTitle: What a mid-level answer looks like: correct, standard patterns
slides.markdown:
A solid mid-level answer applies standard, well-known patterns correctly: the right kind of database for the access pattern, a cache where reads clearly dominate, sensible component boundaries. It's the floor every level is expected to clear, and it's genuinely enough to pass a mid-level bar on its own.

What a mid-level answer typically doesn't include, and isn't expected to: unprompted discussion of what happens when a component fails, why this specific trade-off beats the alternative for this problem, or how the design would evolve as the system's scale or organization changes.

There's no shame in a mid-level answer at a mid-level interview — the mismatch only becomes a problem when it's given at a level expecting more.

slides.sectionTitle: What a senior answer adds: trade-off ownership, edge cases, failure modes
slides.markdown:
A senior answer keeps the same correct core and adds **ownership of the trade-off**: naming the alternative that was rejected and defending the choice under pushback, unprompted discussion of what happens when a dependency is slow or down, and naming edge cases the interviewer didn't ask about but that a real production system would hit.

For a rate limiter, a mid-level answer might correctly propose a token bucket. A senior answer adds: what happens when the rate-limiting service itself is unreachable — fail open or fail closed, and why that choice depends on whether the protected resource is a login endpoint or a public read API.

The throughline is **anticipation** — surfacing the failure modes and trade-offs before being asked, not just answering well when pushed.

slides.sectionTitle: What a staff+ answer adds: organizational/product judgment, cost, migration paths
slides.markdown:
A staff+ answer keeps everything from the senior answer and adds judgment that extends past the system's technical boundary: which team would own and operate each new component, what it costs to run and whether that cost is justified by the problem's actual stakes, and how an org gets from its current system to this one without a risky big-bang cutover.

For the rate limiter, a staff+ answer might note that centralizing rate limiting in a shared service creates a new dependency every team now relies on, discuss whether that's worth the operational cost versus a simpler per-service limit, and sketch a migration path that rolls it out to one service at a time rather than all at once.

This is the [staff-level signal](staff-level-system-design-signal) covered in its own topic — here, the point is simply that it's an addition on top of the senior layer, not a replacement for it.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the same question answered at three depths
slides.markdown:
![Three concentric rings: Mid-level core, Senior adds trade-off ownership, Staff+ adds org judgment](assets/leveling-concentric-rings.svg)

The three levels aren't three different designs — they're the same correct core with additional rings of judgment layered on top. A staff+ answer that skipped the correct core wouldn't score as staff+; it would just be wrong.

This is why leveling up is additive: strengthen the inner ring first, then add the next one, rather than skipping straight to organizational commentary on a design that isn't solid yet.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: breadth vs depth expectations by level
slides.markdown:
Levels differ not just in depth on one component, but in how far the expected view extends outward from the diagram itself.

| Level | Expected focus | Typical follow-up they should pre-empt |
|---|---|---|
| Mid-level | This component, done correctly | "Does this actually work?" |
| Senior | This component's trade-offs and failure modes | "What happens when it fails, and why this over the alternative?" |
| Staff+ | This component's fit within the org and its cost over time | "Who owns this, what does it cost, how do we get there?" |

**How to decide:** before the interview, confirm which level you're being evaluated for, and deliberately pre-empt that level's typical follow-up rather than waiting for it to be asked.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a senior candidate giving a mid-level answer — technically fine, but thin
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My design is correct and clean, so it should score well regardless of the level I'm interviewing for."

**Why it's wrong:** a correct, standard-pattern design that never surfaces a trade-off, a failure mode, or an edge case is exactly a mid-level answer — and at a senior bar, "correct but thin" reads as a candidate who can execute a known pattern but hasn't shown the judgment the level requires. The design isn't wrong; it's just missing the layer being evaluated.

**Correct model:** know which level you're being assessed against before you start, and deliberately narrate the extra layer that level expects — trade-offs and failure modes for senior, organizational and cost judgment for staff+ — rather than assuming a clean diagram speaks for itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: what estimate each level is expected to get right
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
Levels differ concretely in what estimate an interviewer expects to be right. A mid-level candidate is expected to get the QPS and storage math roughly right when given the inputs. A senior candidate is expected to also reason about the estimate's sensitivity — what happens at 10x, where the bottleneck moves first. A staff candidate is expected to connect the estimate to a cost and org decision: "at this write volume, a managed database costs roughly $X/month more than self-hosting, and that's worth flagging to the team before committing."

Concrete example: given "500M daily active users, each posts twice a day," a mid-level answer computes ~11,500 writes/sec average. A senior answer adds that peak is likely 3-5x average, so provision for ~50,000 writes/sec, and names sharding as the fix. A staff answer adds that at that volume, the choice between a managed sharded database and self-managed Cassandra is now a real cost-vs-ops-burden decision worth surfacing.

The takeaway: the number itself is the mid-level bar; what you build on top of the number is what separates the levels.

slides.sectionTitle: Staff-level nuance: calibrating your answer's depth to the interviewer's signal
slides.markdown:
Because the same question can be answered correctly at three different depths, a candidate has to calibrate their own answer's depth against what the interviewer is signaling, not just aim for "as deep as possible." If the interviewer nods and moves on after your mid-level answer, going deeper anyway burns time the interview doesn't have. If they lean in and ask "what would you actually do differently at 10x that scale," that is an explicit invitation to go to the senior or staff layer.

A useful habit: after giving the first-pass answer, pause briefly rather than immediately volunteering the deeper layer — the interviewer's reaction (a follow-up question vs. a nod) tells you whether the deeper answer is wanted right now.

**Testing:** whether you can read the room and match the depth the interviewer is actually asking for, rather than performing a fixed depth regardless of signal.
